title: Rethinking User Delight
intro: Delight is on every OKR and job posting, but rarely defined. Teams paste it on at the end — cheeky microcopy, celebratory animations — while the flow underneath still doesn't work.

learn.title: Delight is not decoration
learn.text:
Teams treat delight as a layer you add on top:
→ Cheeky loading messages
→ Confetti after completing a form
→ Playful microcopy in error states
→ Visual polish on a confusing task flow

These touches can actually **hurt** usability and accessibility. And they don't fix the underlying problem.

If the checkout flow takes 7 steps when it should take 3, no amount of confetti will make users feel delighted.

right.label: What delight actually is
items: The task was hard, now it's easy

try.q: A PM asks you to 'add delight' to a slow, confusing settings page. What's the right first move?
options: Reduce the effort — cut steps, simplify decisions, speed up the page
Add friendly illustrations and microcopy
Design a celebratory animation for when settings are saved
Add a progress bar to show how much is left
try.explain: Reduce effort before adding anything new. Delight emerges from interaction quality, not decoration.

learn.title: Bill Scott's 'interesting moments'
learn.text:
Bill Scott's concept reframes delight as **interaction quality.** Delight comes from small moments where the system:

→ **Prevents errors** before they happen
→ **Gives timely feedback** so users know where they stand
→ **Maintains continuity** so context isn't lost
→ **Reduces effort** by removing unnecessary steps

Users don't consciously notice delight mid-task. They experience it as smooth, low-effort, responsive, and predictable. It's what happens when everything just works.

Well-timed, supportive transitions keep users in a flow state. Decorative ones knock them out of it.

try.q: A form auto-saves as you type, preventing data loss. Is this 'delight'?
options: Yes — it prevents errors and reduces effort, which is real delight
No — delight needs to be visible and celebratory
No — it's just good engineering
Only if users consciously notice and appreciate it
try.explain: This is a textbook 'interesting moment.' Users may not notice it, but they'd sure notice if it was gone.

learn.title: The rule of thumb
learn.text:
**"Reduce effort before adding anything new."**

Before you add a single animation, illustration, or microcopy flourish:

1. Remove unnecessary steps
2. Consolidate decisions
3. Cut unnecessary confirmations
4. Speed up system responses
5. Prevent errors instead of handling them

Then — and only then — consider whether decorative touches add value.

Animations aren't inherently bad. Helpful ones respond to user action, communicate system status, and end quickly. Decorative ones that exist mainly to feel 'modern' are the problem.

Treat delight as something that **emerges from interaction quality**, not something you paste on at the end.

options: A brief transition that shows a new item sliding into a list after 'Add'
A 3-second logo animation on every page load
Parallax scrolling on a settings page
A bouncing arrow pointing to the CTA
try.explain: It responds to user action, communicates that the item was added, and ends immediately. That's an interesting moment.

test.q: According to this framework, what is user delight?
options: An outcome that emerges from interaction quality — smooth, low-effort, responsive systems
Visual polish and aesthetic appeal
Celebratory moments after task completion
High NPS scores and positive reviews
test.explain: Delight isn't a layer you add. It's what users experience when the interaction is smooth, responsive, and effortless.

test.q: What should you do BEFORE adding any decorative touches to a flow?
options: Reduce effort — remove steps, consolidate decisions, cut confirmations
Run an A/B test on different animations
Survey users about what would 'delight' them
Benchmark competitor decorative patterns
test.explain: Reduce effort before adding anything new. You can't decorate your way out of a confusing flow.

test.q: A user finishes a 12-step onboarding flow and sees confetti. They say they liked it in a survey. What's the problem?
options: The flow is 12 steps — reducing it to 4 would create more delight than any confetti
Nothing — the confetti is working
Confetti is bad for accessibility
Surveys can't measure delight
test.explain: Users may like confetti, but they'd like a 4-step flow more. Real delight comes from reducing effort, not celebrating its end.

test.q: What makes an animation helpful rather than decorative?
options: It responds to a user action, communicates status, and ends quickly
It uses the latest CSS techniques
It matches the brand guidelines
It plays on every page load for consistency
test.explain: Helpful animations are triggered by user action, carry information, and don't overstay. Decorative ones play on their own and add nothing.

test.q: Why do users not consciously notice 'real' delight during a task?
options: Because delight in this sense IS the flow state — you only notice when something breaks it
Because users have low attention spans
Because delight is subconscious by definition
Because good design is invisible to non-designers
test.explain: Delight is experienced as smooth, low-effort interaction. You notice friction, not flow. That's the whole point.
